candidate.rationale: Program Namespace System is nearly pure code nomenclature, which is useful for an identity run focused on package, module, and config grammar.

candidate.etymology: Acronym of Queue Control Program.
known_concerns: Queue framing collapses the product toward orchestration and the acronym is generic.
candidate.rationale: Queue Control Program tests how far job-routing language can stretch toward declared LM programs and measurable optimization loops.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from code plus ns, a common abbreviation for namespace, separated by a slash.
known_concerns: The slash fails across Hex and module identifiers and is awkward to say aloud.
candidate.rationale: Looks like a literal namespace token someone might actually type into docs, tickets, or protocol notes when discussing code-owned LM programs.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from the ordinary verb call plus URI scheme punctuation.
known_concerns: It looks like a transport endpoint or RPC scheme rather than a library identity.
candidate.rationale: Treats calling as the central verb and dresses it in URI syntax, which is evocative for adapters and runtime boundaries.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from prog, a common shorthand for program, plus beam with a double-colon separator borrowed from programming syntax.
known_concerns: The syntax is illegible to many non-Elixir audiences and unusable as a direct package identifier.
candidate.rationale: Packs program identity and runtime home into a familiar systems separator that works in protocol discussion even if not in package managers.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from LM, the common initialism, plus run separated by a dot.
known_concerns: The generic LM token and dotted form make searchability and spoken identity weak.
candidate.rationale: Reads like a minimal command or root namespace for language-model programs that are meant to be called rather than merely configured.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from OTP plus loop in URI-scheme form.
known_concerns: It implies a transport or public protocol scheme and will confuse package naming.
candidate.rationale: Explores the idea of OTP as an addressable execution substrate for loops, evaluators, and supervised tools.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from the abbreviation ns and the verb call joined by dot notation.
known_concerns: NS is ambiguous between namespace and nanoseconds, and the dotted form still hurts portability.
candidate.rationale: Makes namespace and call the two irreducible code actions at the center of the system.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from mod as module shorthand, an arrow operator, and run.
known_concerns: The arrow implies a deterministic one-way transformation stronger than the actual runtime guarantees.
candidate.rationale: Feels like a diagrammatic note for how declared modules turn into runnable LM programs, which is close to the project's teaching sequence.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from run and ctrl, a common abbreviation for control, joined by dot notation.
known_concerns: Ctrl shorthand is efficient for operators but poor in speech and teaching materials.
candidate.rationale: Compresses operation and control into a terse systems label that would read naturally on dashboards, traces, and log prefixes.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from beam and prog in URI form.
known_concerns: It looks like a locator or transport URL, not a library or Hex package.
candidate.rationale: Tests a full BEAM-addressing posture where programs are something you locate and invoke on a runtime substrate.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from the noun artifact prefixed by double-colon punctuation borrowed from programming syntax.
known_concerns: Leading punctuation fails across nearly every naming surface and accessibility setting.
candidate.rationale: Pushes the artifact horizon to the front with bare syntax, intentionally treating the name as protocol marker before spoken brand.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from call plus mesh using dot notation.
known_concerns: It is likely to be mistaken for a service mesh or RPC fabric.
candidate.rationale: Suggests many callable components tied together by explicit routing and measurable interconnections.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from prog plus beam joined with at-sign syntax commonly used for hosts and scopes.
known_concerns: The at-sign evokes email or remote host semantics more than a durable library identity.
candidate.rationale: Feels like a scoped execution location where program logic lives at the BEAM boundary rather than inside provider-specific SDKs.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from run and stack using URI punctuation.
known_concerns: It reads like deployment infrastructure and not like a package users would depend on.
candidate.rationale: A scheme-like surface for a stack of runnable artifacts, useful in protocol sketches and intentionally awkward as a formal name.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from task plus ctrl abbreviation joined by dot notation.
known_concerns: Task framing can shrink the broader artifact-optimization horizon.
candidate.rationale: Keeps control vocabulary grounded in everyday task execution, making it legible to operators and product engineers.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from the abbreviation ns and route with a double-colon separator.
known_concerns: Stacked separators and abbreviation density make it poor for speech, docs, and Hex identifiers.
candidate.rationale: Combines namespace and route into a protocol sketch that is close to how people annotate systems diagrams and adapter boundaries.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from call and trace joined by dot notation.
known_concerns: It may over-tilt the identity toward observability instead of declared programs.
candidate.rationale: Connects invocation with measurement and aftermath, which is strong for a system built around evaluation and optimizer lineage.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from beam and run with slash-one borrowed from Elixir function arity syntax.
known_concerns: The cleverness is high but nearly every non-Elixir naming surface rejects the slash form.
candidate.rationale: Uses explicit BEAM and Elixir arity notation to signal callable program units with a strong code-native wink.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from LM and graph in URI-like syntax.
known_concerns: The generic LM prefix and scheme syntax make it feel infrastructural rather than ownable.
candidate.rationale: Frames LM programs as nodes in an addressable graph of calls, tools, and feedback paths.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from prog and ctrl, both conventional technical abbreviations, separated by a dot.
known_concerns: Abbreviation density makes the identity cryptic for newcomers and procurement readers.
candidate.rationale: A terse operator-facing compound that could sit on telemetry prefixes, config trees, or incident logs without much ceremony.

candidate.etymology: Constructed from run and eval joined by a left-arrow operator common in sketches and notebooks.
known_concerns: Arrow syntax is invalid in most identifiers and may imply dataflow or assignment semantics that are not intended.
candidate.rationale: Names the loop between execution and measurement explicitly, using an intentionally diagrammatic arrow that refuses smooth brand polish.

candidate.etymology: Plain-English compound of program and namespace.
known_concerns: It is so generic that searchability and distinctiveness are weak.
candidate.rationale: Almost painfully literal, which is a virtue if the goal is honest code nomenclature that can anchor Hex, docs, telemetry, and module families.

candidate.etymology: Plain-English compound of callable and runtime.
known_concerns: It sounds more like a subsystem or whitepaper heading than a project name.
candidate.rationale: Keeps the core promise narrow and true: declared things can be called inside an explicit runtime.

candidate.etymology: Compound of artifact from research and build provenance language with control plane from distributed systems.
known_concerns: Control plane can overstate current product scope and enterprise ambition.
candidate.rationale: Describes the layer that measures, routes, revises, and releases text or code artifacts with a credible operations horizon.

candidate.etymology: Compound of execution with topology from network and graph theory.
known_concerns: Topology feels analytical and cluster-oriented rather than approachable to ordinary users.
candidate.rationale: Frames programs as nodes in an execution layout whose shape matters for supervision, tools, evaluation, and recomposition.

candidate.etymology: Compound of feedback from control theory with compiler from programming-language tooling.
known_concerns: Compiler is an overpowered term that risks false claims about static semantics or proof.
candidate.rationale: Makes the optimization loop central and insists that feedback is something compiled back into better runnable artifacts.

candidate.etymology: Compound of module with transport from networking and logistics.
known_concerns: Transport suggests a network or serialization library rather than LM programming.
candidate.rationale: Works as a dry but serviceable label for moving declared modules, traces, and artifacts across boundaries and subsystems.

candidate.etymology: Compound of runtime with dispatch from routing and scheduling vocabulary.
known_concerns: The phrase is generic and collides with many scheduling or router concepts.
candidate.rationale: Feels at home in ops language where runnable units are scheduled, supervised, and sent through explicit handlers.

candidate.etymology: Compound of composition with bus from hardware and messaging systems.
known_concerns: Bus metaphors imply a central backbone the product does not strictly require.
candidate.rationale: Expresses modular assembly in terms of a shared carrier for calls, tool results, and evaluation signals.

candidate.etymology: Compound of optimization with backplane from modular hardware interconnects.
known_concerns: Backplane is precise for some engineers and opaque for many others.
candidate.rationale: Gives the artifact-improvement horizon a solid systems metaphor without drifting into universal-agent language.

candidate.etymology: Compound of control with freight from cargo logistics.
known_concerns: The tone is cold, supply-chain heavy, and weak for community adoption.
candidate.rationale: Intentionally bureaucratic language for shipping control signals and improved artifacts through a system of gates and checks.

candidate.etymology: Compound of program with router from network routing.
known_concerns: Router immediately evokes web or networking frameworks.
candidate.rationale: A dry but workable phrase for a system that directs calls, tools, evaluators, and optimizers across named program surfaces.

candidate.etymology: Compound of trace with switchboard from manual call-routing systems.
known_concerns: The operator metaphor is vivid but old-fashioned.
candidate.rationale: Treats traces as first-class things to connect, inspect, and redirect rather than disposable debug exhaust.

candidate.etymology: Plain-English compound of declared and runtime.
known_concerns: It reads like a standards term or academic subtitle more than a distinctive identity.
candidate.rationale: Stays unusually close to the product boundary by saying the runtime exists to execute declared program shapes.

candidate.etymology: Compound of supervision from OTP practice with topology from systems analysis.
known_concerns: The focus is so runtime-specific that optimization and artifacts recede.
candidate.rationale: Leans hard into OTP vocabulary, making failure structure and runtime arrangement part of the name itself.

candidate.etymology: Compound of namespace with chassis from mechanical and electronics framing.
known_concerns: Chassis suggests scaffolding or vehicle hardware more than a living software library.
candidate.rationale: Treats the namespace as the frame that carries modules, tasks, traces, and configuration across later product growth.

candidate.etymology: Compound of artifact with pipeline from build and operations tooling.
known_concerns: Pipeline makes interactive calling and branching control loops feel secondary.
candidate.rationale: Directly names a flow of creation, evaluation, revision, and release across multiple artifact types, including code and text.

candidate.etymology: Compound of loop with dispatcher from scheduling and routing vocabulary.
known_concerns: It sounds like a queue runner or scheduler rather than a declarative LM system.
candidate.rationale: Frames control loops as explicit things that can be routed, restarted, throttled, and inspected.

candidate.etymology: Compound of program with telemetry from remote measurement and observability.
known_concerns: Telemetry is only one aspect of the system and may mislead users about the core API.
candidate.rationale: Centers measurement as a named plane of the product, which plays well in docs, logs, and platform discussions.

candidate.etymology: Compound of runtime with handover from operations and logistics language.
known_concerns: The phrase feels more like incident or shift-management procedure than library identity.
candidate.rationale: Highlights explicit transfer between program stages, tools, humans, and supervised workers without pretending the loop is fully autonomous.

candidate.etymology: Compound of compile from language tooling with logistics from routing and coordination.
known_concerns: Compile and logistics together sound bureaucratic and over-mechanized.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately dry compound for the movement of declared programs through evaluation, optimization, packaging, and release.

candidate.etymology: Compound of forklift from warehouse machinery with namespace from programming.
known_concerns: Forklift suggests migration tooling or bulk moves more than callable LM programs.
candidate.rationale: Imagines the namespace as heavy equipment for lifting and relocating program pieces, which is absurd enough to surface hidden logistics assumptions.

candidate.etymology: Plain-English phrase built from warehouse and programs.
known_concerns: The phrase is far too long for many identifiers and collapses the product into storage.
candidate.rationale: Pushes storage and staging language to the front, testing whether the system feels more like inventory management than execution.

candidate.etymology: Compound of container from shipping and software deployment with prefix from naming systems.
known_concerns: Docker and container-runtime associations will dominate interpretation.
candidate.rationale: Pairs modern deployment vocabulary with namespace grammar, hinting at package families and runtime packaging at once.

candidate.etymology: Phrase built from LM initialism plus traffic control from transportation and operations.
known_concerns: Policing and air-traffic connotations can feel domineering and over-operational.
candidate.rationale: Treats LM programs as things that must be sequenced, gated, and rerouted under load rather than generated and forgotten.

candidate.etymology: Compound of switchyard from rail logistics with gospel from religious proclamation.
known_concerns: Religious baggage and ironic tone make it hard to sustain professionally.
candidate.rationale: Mashes rail routing with doctrinal language, a deliberate category error that tests how moralized protocol talk can sound.

candidate.etymology: Compound of signal from control systems with depot from transport logistics.
known_concerns: It can be mistaken for monitoring, message broker, or radio hardware.
candidate.rationale: Treats signals, traces, and control messages as things that arrive and depart through a managed station.

candidate.etymology: Compound of namespace with customs from border and trade administration.
known_concerns: The state-border metaphor can feel exclusionary, nationalist, or bureaucratic.
candidate.rationale: Frames boundaries between packages, modules, and tool protocols as checkpoints where declarations are inspected before entry.

candidate.etymology: Compound of program with pallet from freight handling.
known_concerns: Pallet implies inert goods more than live callable systems.
candidate.rationale: Makes program artifacts sound like cargo arranged for movement and batching, which honestly matches some optimizer and release workflows.

candidate.etymology: Compound of router from networking with choir from collective performance.
known_concerns: The choral imagery is whimsical enough to undercut the serious code-facing brief.
candidate.rationale: Imagines many routing voices staying in tune, a soft category error for modular systems that coordinate without a single solo agent.

candidate.etymology: Compound of module with warehouse from storage logistics.
known_concerns: Static inventory language conflicts with live runtime behavior and the phrase is dull.
candidate.rationale: Treats modules as stock to be stored, picked, and shipped into runnable programs, an intentionally ungainly industrial metaphor.

candidate.etymology: Compound of control with warehouse from logistics.
known_concerns: It reads like industrial process software rather than LM program tooling.
candidate.rationale: Pushes the control-plane idea into literal storage and handling, which can clarify operational bias by overdoing it.

candidate.etymology: Compound of freight from cargo logistics with compiler from programming-language tooling.
known_concerns: Both halves carry strong existing technical meaning and the combination is hard to interpret honestly.
candidate.rationale: A sharp category error that asks whether artifacts are better imagined as cargo compiled into more useful cargo movements.

candidate.etymology: Compound of protocol with dock from ports and logistics.
known_concerns: Dock language suggests plugin hubs or container platforms more than program identity.
candidate.rationale: Makes protocols feel like places where tools, modules, and artifacts attach under explicit operating rules.

candidate.etymology: Compound of telemetry from observability with orchard from cultivation.
known_concerns: The orchard half softens the code-namespace brief and may read decorative.
candidate.rationale: Crosses measurement with cultivation so that traces and metrics feel tended rather than merely harvested.

candidate.etymology: Compound of namespace with turnstile from access and transit systems.
known_concerns: Turnstile implies gatekeeping or access-control guarantees the library does not make.
candidate.rationale: Frames entry into named module and protocol spaces as something metered, observable, and not automatically open.

candidate.etymology: Compound of program with crane from lifting equipment and docks.
known_concerns: The concrete machinery metaphor is memorable but stiff and oddly literal.
candidate.rationale: Uses a heavy-lift object for programs that must be moved, recomposed, or hoisted across stages without hand-waving the machinery.

candidate.etymology: Compound of artifact with rail from transport infrastructure.
known_concerns: Rail implies one path and may collide with Rails or railway toolchains.
candidate.rationale: Suggests fixed routes for moving artifacts through declared stages of evaluation, optimization, and release.

candidate.etymology: Compound of runtime with dry port, a logistics term for inland cargo terminals linked to seaports.
known_concerns: Dry port is obscure to most developers and carries a static facility image.
candidate.rationale: Borrows a precise logistics term for inland staging and inspection, mapping it onto supervised runtime coordination away from the model endpoint.

candidate.etymology: Compound of loop with tollbooth from roads and metered passage.
known_concerns: Toll language suggests payment, artificial friction, or arbitrary blockage.
candidate.rationale: Treats every optimization or tool loop as something that can be checked, metered, and slowed before proceeding.

candidate.etymology: Compound of namespace with tariff from trade regulation.
known_concerns: Tariff language is adversarial, bureaucratic, and almost impossible to make likable as a package name.
candidate.rationale: Ends in a deliberately abrasive trade metaphor for the cost and friction introduced by namespace boundaries, adapters, and declared interfaces.

run.method: plain language newcomer conversation

candidate.etymology: English verb from Latin declarare, to make clear or announce.
candidate.grammar: ordinary verb and command
known_concerns: Declare can sound like a static guarantee or a command to a compiler, neither of which is the whole product.
candidate.rationale: A newcomer can remember the action: say what the program should do before calling it. It points to explicit signatures without claiming that the language model itself becomes certain.

candidate.etymology: English phrase built from the ordinary verb call and the pronoun it.
candidate.grammar: short imperative phrase
known_concerns: The phrase is common in speech and may be hard to own or distinguish from a telephone or marketing call to action.
candidate.rationale: It gives a teachable sentence: call the program with these inputs. It makes the callable boundary memorable while leaving room for evaluation and optimization after the call.

candidate.etymology: English phrase from keeping a written score in games and contests.
candidate.grammar: short imperative phrase
known_concerns: Score language can reduce care and judgment to one number or suggest competitive rankings the project does not promise.
candidate.rationale: It explains metrics plainly: a program is not called better because it sounds better; examples and scores show what changed. It also separates this library from a hosted chatbot that hides its evaluation process.

candidate.etymology: English adjective plain joined to the ordinary software noun programs.
candidate.grammar: descriptive plural noun phrase
known_concerns: Plain can imply simplistic behavior, plain text only, or a value judgment against more advanced users.
candidate.rationale: It says the teaching goal out loud: programs should be explainable as declared, callable work rather than mysterious prompt strings. The plural can cover signatures, calls, metrics, and optimizers without becoming a hosted service name.

candidate.etymology: English polite request using please, do not, and automate.
candidate.grammar: polite negative imperative
known_concerns: The negative joke may sound hostile to useful automation and could be mistaken for a political or safety campaign.
candidate.rationale: This joke-like anti-brand makes the boundary memorable: a library can expose actions and tools without taking responsibility away from people. It invites a teammate to ask what is declared and measured before calling something autonomous.

candidate.etymology: English phrase using teach in its ordinary sense of showing through examples and practice.
candidate.grammar: imperative phrase
known_concerns: Teach can anthropomorphize the model or imply learning that continues automatically without an explicit optimization run.
candidate.rationale: It gives a newcomer a concrete story: provide examples, run the program, inspect results, and improve the artifact. It avoids saying the model is a child while keeping apprenticeship as a human activity.

candidate.etymology: English phrase combining program with receipts as records of a transaction or result.
candidate.grammar: descriptive phrase with ordinary object
known_concerns: Receipts can imply complete auditability, preserved personal data, or financial accounting beyond the actual implementation.
candidate.rationale: It makes traces, examples, metrics, and optimizer lineage easy to explain: the program can show what was tried and how it was judged. That is a useful difference from a hosted AI product that presents only a final answer.

candidate.etymology: English noun phrase using contract for an explicit agreement and small for limited scope.
candidate.grammar: descriptive noun phrase
known_concerns: Contract may carry legal or formal-verification expectations, while small may undersell larger artifact optimization work.
candidate.rationale: It teaches that a signature is a small, visible agreement about inputs and outputs, not a proof that a model will obey. The name is easy to put in a sentence about making one task callable.

candidate.etymology: English verbs arranged as a plain sequence of experiment, evaluation, and revision.
candidate.grammar: three-part imperative phrase
known_concerns: The rhythm can sound like a universal optimization recipe even though outcomes depend on data, metrics, and model behavior.
candidate.rationale: The phrase is a complete newcomer explanation of the loop: run an attempt, measure it, then revise the program artifact. It keeps improvement grounded in work rather than promising an independently improving machine.

candidate.etymology: English adjective boring plus the phrase on purpose.
candidate.grammar: short explanatory phrase
known_concerns: Boring can be read as dull, underpowered, or dismissive of research and creative uses.
candidate.rationale: This anti-hype joke signals that explicit data, ordinary functions, and visible failure are features. It helps a newcomer distinguish a library checked into an Elixir project from a glossy hosted AI product.

candidate.etymology: English compound hand plus off, describing the transfer of work or responsibility.
candidate.grammar: ordinary noun and command noun
known_concerns: Handoff is already common in operations and care work, so the name may feel generic or suggest workflow software only.
candidate.rationale: It makes a useful sentence easy: the program hands a prediction to the next measured step or to a person. It keeps agency and responsibility visible instead of implying that a hosted agent owns the whole task.

candidate.etymology: English idiom for a practical rough guide, with disputed historical stories; no precise origin is claimed here.
candidate.grammar: ordinary idiom
known_concerns: The idiom has disputed histories and can be inaccessible internationally; it may also sound less precise than an engineering library should be.
candidate.rationale: It communicates a teachable heuristic without dressing it up as a theorem. It could frame examples and metrics as practical guides while respecting that model behavior remains uncertain.

candidate.etymology: English phrase using little as a modest quantity and help as assistance.
candidate.grammar: short phrase
known_concerns: Little help may undersell a serious engineering library and could be heard as a promise of safe assistance.
candidate.rationale: It offers a humane way to describe bounded model assistance: a declared program helps with a task, but it does not replace the person or own the outcome. The modest scale is memorable to newcomers.

candidate.etymology: English classroom instruction asking a learner to display the steps behind an answer.
candidate.grammar: imperative phrase
known_concerns: The phrase can imply access to private model reasoning or a requirement to expose sensitive traces, neither of which is guaranteed.
candidate.rationale: It is immediately teachable: keep the inputs, calls, scores, and changed artifacts visible enough for a teammate to inspect. It distinguishes an evidence-bearing program from a service that returns only a response.

candidate.etymology: English phrase from control and automation discussions about a person participating in a process.
candidate.grammar: common noun phrase
known_concerns: The phrase is jargon-heavy and can reduce people to a safety checkpoint rather than recognizing their expertise and labor.
candidate.rationale: It names a boundary a newcomer can understand: people decide what is allowed, what counts as good, and what happens after a result. The phrase keeps the product from being confused with a fully hosted autonomous agent.

candidate.etymology: English imperative using ask and the number twice.
candidate.grammar: short imperative phrase
known_concerns: Twice is an arbitrary number and may suggest that two trials establish reliability.
candidate.rationale: It makes evaluation memorable: do not trust one lucky answer; try the declared program against more than one example or check. It is also a gentle reminder that a model answer is not a final authority.

candidate.etymology: English phrase describing a result that meets a stated practical bar rather than an absolute ideal.
candidate.grammar: descriptive noun phrase
known_concerns: Good enough can sound careless in high-stakes settings or obscure who sets the acceptable metric.
candidate.rationale: It gives product teams plain language for metric-driven improvement: choose a bar, measure it, and know what remains imperfect. It resists the claim that optimization produces universally best behavior.

candidate.etymology: English noun book paired with example as a worked case or data row.
candidate.grammar: ordinary object phrase
known_concerns: Book imagery can narrow the product to writing or imply that examples are static lessons rather than evaluation data.
candidate.rationale: It gives newcomers a physical picture for examples, dev sets, and demonstrations: a program learns its intended shape from cases people can read and discuss. It is clearly a library artifact, not a hosted AI marketplace.

candidate.etymology: English proverb-like phrase adapted from measure twice, cut once.
candidate.grammar: short imperative phrase
known_concerns: The woodworking source phrase may feel like craft branding and can imply that every problem has one correct cut.
candidate.rationale: It teaches a cautious optimization loop: inspect the metric and examples before changing an artifact. The phrase is memorable without claiming that measurement removes uncertainty.

candidate.etymology: English phrase denying that the product is a wand that produces instant results.
candidate.grammar: negative noun phrase and joke
known_concerns: The joke can make the project sound unserious and may be too negative for a master brand.
candidate.rationale: This category error is an honest anti-promise: the library organizes declared work, calls, metrics, and revisions, while people still provide judgment and model access. It is easy to repeat to a teammate who expects a hosted shortcut.

candidate.etymology: English imperative phrase using let and try for bounded experimentation.
candidate.grammar: short imperative phrase
known_concerns: Let it try can sound like permission to make real-world changes without a clear tool or review boundary.
candidate.rationale: It expresses an experiment without granting the program unrestricted authority: let a declared call try, then inspect its result. That is a simple bridge from play to measurable software work.

candidate.etymology: A playful English formation from explainable plus the suffix-ish, openly weakening the claim.
candidate.grammar: humorous coined adjective
known_concerns: The joke can weaken trust, and explainable remains a loaded claim for buyers and affected people.
candidate.rationale: The modest suffix makes a useful teaching point: traces and artifacts can make behavior easier to inspect, but they do not turn a language model into a fully explained machine. It is memorable because it admits the limit.

candidate.etymology: English adjective ordinary paired with the software noun program.
candidate.grammar: descriptive noun phrase
known_concerns: Ordinary may erase the special uncertainty of language models or sound like the project has no research ambition.
candidate.rationale: It says the intended teaching stance: a language-model program should have inputs, outputs, calls, tests, and configuration like other software. It helps newcomers distinguish a code library from a hosted chat product.

candidate.etymology: English verbs arranged as a short cycle of execution, observation, and repair.
candidate.grammar: three-part imperative phrase
known_concerns: Fix implies that failures have one obvious repair and can make the process sound more automatic than it is.
candidate.rationale: A teammate can repeat the workflow in one breath: run the program, see the measured result, and fix the artifact or data. It names practical improvement without promising a self-improving engine.

candidate.etymology: English phrase for alternating participation in a game or conversation.
candidate.grammar: ordinary imperative phrase
known_concerns: Turn-taking can make concurrent or supervised BEAM work sound strictly sequential and may imply equal agency where there is none.
candidate.rationale: It offers a humane picture of model, tool, and person participation: each turn has a boundary and a handoff. It also makes an accessible distinction from an agent promised to act continuously on its own.

candidate.etymology: English compound naming a belt used to carry hand tools.
candidate.grammar: ordinary object phrase
known_concerns: Tool imagery can suggest manual construction, a fixed tool set, or physical safety rather than explicit software boundaries.

candidate.grammar: descriptive category phrase
known_concerns: The phrase is generic and work language may sound like consulting, labor tracking, or a product with no distinctive identity.
candidate.rationale: It puts the whole explanation in ordinary words: people declare, call, measure, and improve language-model programs as software work. It is broad enough for a credible artifact horizon but not a promise of a universal platform.

candidate.etymology: English conversational apology followed by a common qualification for context-dependent answers.
candidate.grammar: polite hedged phrase and joke
known_concerns: The phrase can sound evasive, indecisive, or too negative for a product that still needs a clear technical account.
candidate.rationale: It is an honest newcomer lesson: model choice, examples, metrics, tools, and boundaries affect what a program can do, so no universal answer or automatic improvement is promised. The joke keeps uncertainty speakable rather than hiding it behind product confidence.
