known_concerns: Possible cross-language meanings and pronunciation differences need later research; it can also sound like a wellness brand.
candidate.rationale: Suggests a circle or roundtable without directly claiming governance, making it a plausible community or artifact-family mark. It can support plurality and feedback loops while staying abstract enough for future scope.

candidate.etymology: Coined sound-symbolic form; resembles zero and oath but has no established etymology.
known_concerns: The fantasy-style sound is likely too grandiose and may imply vows, security, or solemn guarantees.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately overbuilt abstract mark with zero and oath echoes: absence plus commitment. It is useful as a bad-aging stress test because it sounds dramatic while pointing at refusal and negative results.

candidate.etymology: Coined sound-symbolic form with no claimed origin.
known_concerns: The q cluster creates speech and spelling friction, and it may be read as invented exoticism.
candidate.rationale: A compact mark with unusual letter shape that separates identity from explanation. It could remain flexible across library, hosted service, and protocol marks, but it does not itself teach the typed artifact-optimization category.

candidate.etymology: Coined as used here; resembles lumen and light-related roots but no illumination claim is intended.
known_concerns: Light metaphors can imply transparency or truth, and the soft form may be crowded in consumer products.
candidate.rationale: A bright abstract form that could frame inspectability and evidence without saying proof, compiler, or safety. It is easy to say, but that same friendliness may flatten the serious operational boundary work.

candidate.etymology: Coined form; may evoke review, revise, or via, but no specific derivation is claimed.
known_concerns: The review echo may narrow the product to editing or QA, and spelling alternatives are obvious.
candidate.rationale: A review-and-revision flavored abstract mark for optimizer feedback, artifact deltas, and versioned program values. It can age with maintenance practices if not tied too narrowly to one algorithm generation.

candidate.etymology: Coined sound-symbolic form; resembles omni, all, but the all-scope reading is not endorsed.
known_concerns: Omni language risks universal-agent and total-platform claims the atlas excludes.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately dangerous abstract name that hints at omni while ending in low or no. It tests how easily broad artifact optimization can slide into universal-platform overclaiming.

candidate.etymology: Coined form; visually resembles no and nova, new star, but no astronomical claim is intended.
known_concerns: The startup spelling may age badly, and nova associations can imply explosive growth despite the no prefix.
candidate.rationale: A no-plus-nova sound mark that both invites and blocks newness. It probes anti-growth naming for a field obsessed with novelty while still leaving room for a future company brand.

candidate.etymology: Coined sound-symbolic form; may evoke vantablack or veil, but no material or opacity claim is intended.
known_concerns: Darkness and veil associations may suggest opacity, secrecy, or security theater.
candidate.rationale: A dark, spacious abstract mark for negative space, withheld action, and uncertainty. It is broad enough for multiple products but risks drifting into fantasy or cyber-aesthetic branding instead of technical trust.

candidate.etymology: Coined sound-symbolic form with no claimed etymology.
known_concerns: The ending is hard to hear, and the form may be mistaken for a personal or fantasy name.
candidate.rationale: A neutral invented mark that could hold an Elixir-rooted library today and a runtime-neutral artifact system later. Its lack of built-in meaning makes the category descriptor decisive.

candidate.etymology: Coined clipping that resembles probability and problem; no formal statistical term is claimed.
known_concerns: The baby-talk sound may undermine seriousness, and probability echoes can overpromise statistical rigor.
candidate.rationale: A probability-adjacent abstract name for measured uncertainty, held-out evaluation, and non-deterministic behavior. It is intentionally less formal than probability so it cannot pretend to statistical proof.

candidate.etymology: Coined form; may evoke axis, axiom, or maximum, but no exact derivation is claimed.
known_concerns: Axiom-adjacent sound can mislead researchers toward proof claims and may collide with mathematical or enterprise brands.
candidate.rationale: A crisp abstract form that can hint at axes, axioms, and maxima while still requiring explicit scope limits. It tests whether technical resonance can be carried without claiming formal methods or optimizer superiority.

candidate.etymology: Coined form combining repeated z sounds with zeta, the name of the Greek letter.
known_concerns: It looks unserious, is difficult to pronounce, and may imply latency or dormancy as product defects.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately odd sleepy-symbolic mark for pauses, non-action, and final alphabetic position. It stress-tests bad but memorable sound branding for a library that must sometimes do less.

candidate.etymology: Janus is a Roman deity associated with doors, thresholds, beginnings, and transitions.
known_concerns: Mythic naming can feel grandiose, culturally narrow, or misleadingly institutional; Janus also appears in many existing contexts.
candidate.rationale: The two-faced Roman threshold figure can name a system that looks both toward executable Elixir contracts and stochastic model behavior. It is useful for boundary translation and migration, but it must not become a mythic authority claim.

candidate.etymology: Cassandra is a figure from Greek myth associated with true warnings that are not believed.
known_concerns: The myth includes gendered disbelief and trauma, and the name is heavily used in databases and software.
candidate.rationale: A warning-centered name for evaluations that surface failures, drift, and ignored uncertainty before deployment. It challenges optimism but risks making the project sound doomed rather than useful.

candidate.etymology: Ariadne is a Greek mythological figure associated with a thread used to navigate a labyrinth.
known_concerns: The myth can reduce the named figure to a helper object, and pronunciation varies widely.
candidate.rationale: A thread-through-complexity name for traces, optimizer lineage, and multi-step program routes. It can hold retrieval and tool playbooks without claiming to solve every labyrinth of model behavior.

candidate.etymology: Hephaestus is the Greek deity associated with smithing, craft, and making.
known_concerns: The spelling is difficult, the myth has disability and exclusion baggage, and a deity name can sound inflated.
candidate.rationale: A craft-centered mythic name for building tools, adapters, and optimizer artifacts as durable objects. It pushes against pure prompt magic, but it may overpower the modest library boundary.

candidate.etymology: Prometheus is a Greek mythic figure associated with bringing fire; ledger is a record book.
known_concerns: Prometheus language is deeply overused in AI, implies dangerous power, and may invite safety-product or reckless-innovation readings.
candidate.rationale: A grandiose stress test joining fire-bringing myth with accountable records for optimization changes. It probes whether breakthrough language can be tempered by evidence, cost, and lineage, but it probably oversells the system.

candidate.etymology: Solon was an Athenian lawmaker traditionally associated with legal and political reforms.
known_concerns: Historical governance names can sound elitist, patriarchal, or like premature standards authority.
candidate.rationale: A lawgiver name for explicit rules, evaluation gates, and restraint without claiming to be a standards body. It could support governance language for a future community steward, but may feel remote from code.

candidate.etymology: Hypatia was a late antique mathematician and philosopher associated with Alexandria.
known_concerns: The historical violence around Hypatia and the academic aura can overwhelm an Elixir library identity.
candidate.rationale: A scholar-name option for rigorous inquiry, commentary, and teaching across technical artifacts. It emphasizes learning and interpretation but risks appropriating a historical person into a software brand.

candidate.etymology: Zeno refers to ancient Greek philosophers associated with paradoxes; gate is an ordinary boundary object.
known_concerns: Possessive punctuation hurts package ergonomics, and philosophy references can feel exclusionary.
candidate.rationale: A paradox-and-boundary name for incremental improvement that may never reach an absolute optimum. It suits uncertainty and promotion thresholds while warning against guaranteed self-improvement stories.

candidate.etymology: Alan Turing was a foundational figure in computing; margin is an edge, allowance, or spare capacity.
known_concerns: Turing names are crowded and can imply AI benchmarks, theoretical rigor, or borrowed prestige.
candidate.rationale: Uses a historical computing reference while placing the emphasis on the margin, not machine intelligence triumph. It can frame tests, traces, and residual uncertainty, but it must avoid claiming theoretical authority.

candidate.etymology: Babel refers to the biblical story of linguistic confusion; commons means shared resource or community stewardship.
known_concerns: Biblical reference and commons politics carry cultural and ideological baggage, and Babel often connotes failure.
candidate.rationale: A plural-language and shared-governance stress test for a future ecosystem where many runtimes and representations coexist. It acknowledges translation confusion rather than promising one universal language.

candidate.etymology: Delphi refers to the ancient Greek oracle site; null is a technical and ordinary term for no value.
known_concerns: Oracle framing is a major category error for a library that does not know truth or future outcomes.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately contradictory oracle name that returns no answer when evidence is insufficient. It maps to evaluation and refusal, but it must not imply prophecy, official guidance, or model omniscience.

candidate.etymology: Theseus refers to the ship-of-Theseus identity puzzle; index is a pointer, catalog, or ordered reference.
known_concerns: The classical puzzle may be too clever, and index can imply search infrastructure rather than program optimization.
candidate.rationale: A long-term maintenance name for program identity across changing instructions, examples, schemas, and optimizer versions. It is strong for lineage but may make ordinary users solve a philosophy puzzle first.

candidate.etymology: Ada refers to Ada Lovelace; footnote is a publishing annotation.
known_concerns: Using Ada Lovelace as brand material is crowded and may feel extractive; possessive punctuation is code-hostile.
candidate.rationale: A historical-computing phrase that centers annotations, examples, and written program intent around executable artifacts. It can teach the documentation-rich side of the project while avoiding claims of being a new programming language.

candidate.etymology: Ostrom refers to political economist Elinor Ostrom; table is an ordinary meeting or data surface.
known_concerns: It risks borrowing academic authority and may imply the project provides governance frameworks beyond software boundaries.
candidate.rationale: Brings commons governance into conversation with model, tool, and dataset stewardship without claiming to be a governance institute. It can help future community architecture think about rules and accountability.

candidate.etymology: Icarus is a Greek mythic figure associated with overreaching flight; brake is a stopping or slowing mechanism.
known_concerns: It is melodramatic, moralizing, and might imply the product is mainly a safety brake.
candidate.rationale: An anti-hubris name for slowing autonomous escalation before model programs fly beyond evidence, budget, or responsibility. It explicitly tests a name that may age badly because the warning myth is so familiar.

candidate.etymology: Rosetta refers to the Rosetta Stone, a historical artifact associated with decipherment; boundary is an interface or limit.
known_concerns: Rosetta naming is crowded, colonial artifact context matters, and the metaphor can imply lossless translation.
candidate.rationale: A translation-name candidate for turning model messages into typed Elixir values and back while keeping losses explicit. It scales to schemas and tool descriptions but must avoid implying universal translation.

candidate.etymology: Sisyphus is a Greek mythic figure associated with endless labor; release is a software publication event.
known_concerns: The myth strongly connotes futility and punishment, which may repel contributors and buyers.
candidate.rationale: A maintenance-heavy name for repeated optimizer runs, shifting model behavior, and release gates that never end. It is honest about effort but can make the project feel futile.

candidate.etymology: Annales is Latin for annals and names a historical mode associated with long-duration study.
known_concerns: Academic and Latin styling can feel pretentious, and pronunciation or pluralization is not obvious.
candidate.rationale: A long-duration historical name for preserving optimizer evidence, rejected edits, and program changes across years rather than launches. It suits future research archives more than a friendly Hex package.

candidate.etymology: Mnemosyne is a Greek mythological figure associated with memory; archive is a record collection.
known_concerns: The spelling is difficult, mythic memory can sound mystical, and archive can imply retention claims with privacy implications.
candidate.rationale: A memory-and-records name for durable optimization artifacts, traces, and reusable playbook context. It allows a future archival service while demanding care not to confuse memory with truth.

candidate.etymology: Olympus is the mythic home of Greek deities; CI is the software initialism for continuous integration.
known_concerns: The divine scale is absurd for an Elixir library and may imply authoritative certification or superiority.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately overblown name joining divine mountain imagery with continuous integration gates. It stress-tests whether release evidence could become a grand platform myth instead of a humble maintainer tool.

candidate.etymology: Technical symbolic compound from null, no value, slash as separator, and OK as acceptance marker.
known_concerns: Slash and capitalization are poor for package names, and OK may imply acceptance criteria are simpler than they are.
candidate.rationale: A protocol-like mark for explicit non-output and accepted output living side by side. It is compact and machine-readable enough for artifacts, but it needs human-facing descriptors for community and company use.

candidate.etymology: Protocol-style compound from English maybe, colon namespace syntax, and run as execution.
known_concerns: Colon syntax is code-adjacent but awkward in speech, and maybe may sound unreliable to buyers.
candidate.rationale: A symbolic execution mark for a run that proceeds under uncertainty and can still produce abstention, rollback, or evidence. It names runtime humility rather than autonomous certainty.

candidate.etymology: Protocol and namespace style using current DSEx root plus dot notation and not as negation.
known_concerns: It depends on the old name, is not a fresh master identity, and dot syntax is unsuitable for many surfaces.
candidate.rationale: A namespace-led negative mark for refusal paths, unsupported claims, and explicit non-equivalence with official DSPy. It is intentionally close to code and poor as a master brand, preserving a raw category-error observation.

candidate.etymology: Invented protocol mark combining angle, pipe-like separator, and hold as a control word.
known_concerns: It is nearly unspeakable, inaccessible in prose, and too syntax-like for a durable brand.
candidate.rationale: A symbolic pipeline-like mark for interrupting flow before a tool call, promotion, or artifact replacement. It turns BEAM and Elixir pipeline intuition toward pausing rather than forward-only execution.

candidate.etymology: Symbolic form using 0x hexadecimal prefix and English refuse in uppercase.
known_concerns: It reads as an error code, may sound hostile, and can imply a formal protocol specification that does not exist.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately harsh machine mark that turns refusal into a recognizable state code. It is useful for probing legal and security misreadings because it looks like a protocol error more than a product.

candidate.etymology: Invented symbolic form using percent signs as markers and NoPort as a camel-cased phrase.
known_concerns: Too defensive for a main identity and hard to type, say, search, or package.
candidate.rationale: A code-like marker for the explicit claim that the library is not an official or drop-in port. It is a raw maintainer-facing identity fragment, not a polished public name.

candidate.etymology: Protocol-style compound using BEAM as the Erlang VM family name, colon as namespace separator, and many as plurality.
known_concerns: It may be too BEAM-tied for a runtime-neutral future and uppercase protocol style is visually loud.
candidate.rationale: A symbolic architecture mark for BEAM-native implementation with many models, tools, and language ecosystems around it. It keeps Elixir resonance while refusing a single-model or single-provider center.

candidate.etymology: Invented symbol sequence: question mark for uncertainty, arrow for transformation, exclamation for assertion or action.
known_concerns: It is inaccessible, unsearchable, unspeakable, and too close to claiming deterministic transformation.
candidate.rationale: A pure symbolic mark for uncertain input becoming committed output only after program structure, evaluation, and policy. It compresses the credible horizon into one glyph sequence but is almost impossible to explain without legend.

candidate.etymology: Software term fork combined with slash-separated negation.
known_concerns: Fork language may suggest project governance conflict, and slash syntax is weak for a master brand.
candidate.rationale: A protocol-like phrase for choosing whether an artifact lineage should branch or remain stable. It fits optimizer archives, rejected edits, and community governance without claiming one true lifecycle.

candidate.etymology: Symbolic path style modeled on Unix device paths, with maybe as the device name.
known_concerns: Unix joke energy is exclusionary, hard to brand, and may sound like random output rather than evaluated programs.
candidate.rationale: A Unix-flavored category error for a device of uncertainty: values can be generated, withheld, or redirected. It is memorable for developers but intentionally bad for nontechnical audiences.

candidate.etymology: Elixir atom syntax plus epsilon, a Greek letter often used in mathematics for a small quantity.
known_concerns: Greek-letter math can imply formal guarantees and the colon form does not travel well outside Elixir contexts.
candidate.rationale: An atom-like symbolic name for small tolerated differences, residual uncertainty, and improvement thresholds. It is close to Elixir code while reminding users that metrics have margins.

candidate.etymology: Uppercase technical phrase combining eval, or, and stop with hyphen separators.
known_concerns: It can sound like a safety product or compliance gate and may overstate how complete evaluation can be.
candidate.rationale: A loud protocol label for the discipline that optimization and action should pass through evaluation gates or halt. It is procurement-legible but too slogan-like for nuanced research claims.

candidate.etymology: Invented symbolic camel-case form with x as marker and NoProof as negated phrase.
known_concerns: It is defensive, ugly, and might make users think the project lacks rigor rather than avoids false proof claims.
candidate.rationale: A code-fragment-like mark for explicitly excluding formal proof claims while retaining tests, metrics, and typed data. It is useful as adversarial nomenclature because it foregrounds the negative claim too strongly.

candidate.etymology: Invented protocol URI style using plural as scheme-like word and beam as host-like runtime marker.
known_concerns: URI syntax can falsely imply a real protocol or standard and is poor for speech.
candidate.rationale: A URL-like compatibility mark for many artifact forms on a BEAM implementation. It supports a future protocol-ecosystem idea while clearly not being an actual network scheme unless one is later defined.

candidate.etymology: Symbolic uppercase phrase using a question mark and direct negation.
known_concerns: It can read as unsafe, hostile, or flippant, and could create exactly the procurement anxiety it is meant to surface.
candidate.rationale: A deliberately abrasive mark that refuses safety-product positioning and asks whether a system should answer no to the safe label. It is an adversarial legal/security probe, not a recommended public tone.

candidate.etymology: Handle-style at sign plus lineage, descent or provenance.
known_concerns: The at sign suggests social handles or annotations, and lineage can imply inheritance hierarchy rather than explicit provenance.
candidate.rationale: A lightweight symbolic handle for parentage across optimizer candidates, demos, tool descriptions, and retrieved policy artifacts. It works as subsystem nomenclature more than a master brand.

candidate.etymology: Symbolic equation-like form using N as a common count variable and maybe as uncertainty.
known_concerns: It may look unserious to statisticians and unintelligible to users, while equation style suggests more rigor than present.
candidate.rationale: A small statistical-looking mark for sample size, uncertainty, and the fact that evaluation evidence can be insufficient. It pushes against benchmark certainty while remaining too cryptic for general audiences.

candidate.etymology: Protocol-style dot compound from halt, stop execution, and tap, a point for inspection or diversion.
known_concerns: It is subsystem-shaped rather than brand-shaped and may imply runtime interception or security control.
candidate.rationale: A dot-namespaced mark that combines halting with inspection taps in a pipeline. It suggests a code-level subsystem for pausing, tracing, and reviewing optimization or tool execution.

candidate.etymology: Function-call syntax around voidable, an English legal adjective meaning capable of being voided.
known_concerns: Parentheses make it a poor mark, and voidable has legal contract baggage that may imply warranties or remedies.
candidate.rationale: A function-like name for artifacts or actions that can be invalidated, declined, or rolled back when evidence changes. It aligns with maintenance and non-finality but could be too legalistic.

candidate.etymology: Plain English paradox using standard as both shared rule and institutional claim, modified by standardless.
known_concerns: It directly creates standards-body confusion, sounds incoherent, and is nearly unusable as a serious product name.
candidate.rationale: A final category-error protocol name for the tension between wanting shared artifact contracts and refusing standards-body authority. It can provoke useful dissent about future ecosystem architecture, but it is intentionally self-contradictory.

run.brief: Create a schema-version-1 identity portfolio for the pre-release Elixir/OTP library boundary: declared, callable, measurable, optimizable LM programs now, with a credible typed textual and artifact optimization horizon spanning instructions, demonstrations, tool descriptions, retrieval policies, playbooks, schemas, code fragments, and configuration. Do not frame it as an official DSPy port, static proof system, universal agent OS, provider SDK, guaranteed autonomous self-improvement system, safety product, standards body, or institute. Generate exactly 30 contiguous candidates in three owned ten-candidate cells. Cell 1, derivation-clipping, covers declaration-contract and boundary-translation through coined-category-noun and ordinary-verb forms for elixir-newcomers, international-users, and future-maintainers; it contrasts full stem, clipping, elision, prefix, suffix, and conversion and states grammar and dictation risk. Cell 4, conversion-grammar, covers action-agency and care-stewardship-repair through ordinary-verb, ordinary-object, and phrase-imperative forms for affected-publics and backend-product-engineers; it exercises noun, verb, adjective, and command readings and states intended prose and code roles. Cell 7, identity-grammar, covers plurality-ecosystem and infrastructure-logistics through namespace-led, institutional-community, and descriptive-category systems for future-maintainers, buyers-founders, and oss-contributors; each candidate explicitly maps master, descriptor, library, research, community, company, protocol, and product-family roles and marks unavailable roles. Preserve affirmative, odd, adverse, and malformed observations. Use exactly six wildcards, two per cell; cell 1 and cell 7 each use five affirmative, three ambivalent, and two adverse records, while cell 4 uses five affirmative, two ambivalent, and three adverse records. Each cell uses exactly four current, four horizon, and two both scope records. Every candidate requires pronunciation, grammar, honest etymology, valid nonempty audience and architecture lenses, substantive rationale, concerns, and keyed notes for challenge wave, challenge cell, form mechanism, stance, scope, code projection, current embodiment, and horizon embodiment. Every code projection supplies hex, OTP, module, Mix, config, and telemetry forms, or an intentionally non-code role linked to a viable implementation identity. Use atlas IDs only, keep provisional concepts in notes, and avoid default -ex, -ly, -io, AI, LM, bot, and Latinate escape hatches. Do not browse or availability-check.
run.method: isolated morphological matrix: derivation, conversion, identity grammar

candidate.etymology: English 'declare', from Middle English and Latin lineage; an existing ordinary verb, not a coinage.
candidate.grammar: Full-stem ordinary verb; primary prose reading is the command or infinitive 'declare a program', while title-case Declare can convert to a product noun. The verb remains the intended role; noun use is secondary.
known_concerns: Dictation risk: low for the word, but listeners may write 'declar' or assume a generic command rather than a name.
The ordinary verb is crowded and weakly distinctive, and it can suggest stronger contractual guarantees than runtime validation provides.

challenge_cell: 1 derivation-clipping
form_mechanism: full stem retained without affixation; title-case noun use is conversion only
stance: affirmative
scope: current
code_projection: hex=declare; otp=:declare; module=Declare; mix=declare; config=:declare; telemetry=[:declare].
current_embodiment: Declare names signatures and callable Elixir program contracts.
horizon_embodiment: Declare can extend to declared typed parameters for demonstrations, policies, schemas, code fragments, and configuration without claiming that declaration proves correctness.
candidate.rationale: Declare names the present front door accurately: a developer makes inputs, outputs, instructions, and constraints explicit before calling and measuring a program. It is plain enough for newcomers and does not imply compile-time proof.

candidate.etymology: Existing English word with Germanic and French lineages across its limit, leap, and destination senses; this proposal deliberately converts the limit sense into a software identity.
candidate.grammar: Conversion among verb, adjective, and noun: developers bound an action, a tool call is bounded, and a Bound can name the executable boundary object. The intended prose role is verb/adjective; the intended code role is noun namespace.
known_concerns: Dictation risk: medium because 'bound' may be heard as 'bounde' only in spelling recovery and has several unrelated senses.
The adjective can sound restrictive, while the leap and book senses dilute the contract meaning.
notes: challenge_wave: form-saturation-a
challenge_cell: 1 derivation-clipping
form_mechanism: zero-derivation conversion of an ordinary verb/adjective into a category noun
stance: affirmative
scope: current
code_projection: hex=bound; otp=:bound; module=Bound; mix=bound; config=:bound; telemetry=[:bound].
current_embodiment: Bound names runtime-validated task and action boundaries around callable programs.
horizon_embodiment: Bound can organize separately typed and versioned artifact boundaries while keeping execution and optimization limits explicit.
candidate.rationale: Bound foregrounds the honest limit around stochastic behavior and tool use. It is compact, familiar, and close to Elixir's concern with explicit process and effect boundaries without promising static enforcement.

candidate.etymology: Coined by clipping the final syllable from English 'declare'; no external source.
candidate.grammar: Back-clipped coined category noun from 'declare'; it takes ordinary noun syntax ('a Decla program', 'Decla programs') and should not be used as a verb.
known_concerns: Dictation risk: high because DEK-luh may be written Decla, Dekla, or Declaah, and some speakers may stress the second syllable.
The clipping looks unfinished and can read as a typo or an abbreviation with no stable expansion.

challenge_cell: 1 derivation-clipping
form_mechanism: back-clipping declare to decla
stance: affirmative
scope: current
code_projection: hex=decla; otp=:decla; module=Decla; mix=decla; config=:decla; telemetry=[:decla].
current_embodiment: Decla is a compact identity for declared signatures, programs, calls, evaluations, and optimizer reports.
horizon_embodiment: Decla can prefix typed artifact families such as Decla.Policy and Decla.Schema without narrowing the optimized value to prompts.
candidate.rationale: Decla tests whether clipping can preserve declaration semantics while yielding a short package and module root. Its two syllables are lighter than Declaration and leave room for a family of named components.

candidate.etymology: Coined by eliding the first 'e' from English 'declare'; no external source.
candidate.grammar: Vowel-elided coined noun with an optional command echo; intended noun syntax is 'a Dclare program' and code uses title-case Dclare. Treating it as the ordinary verb 'declare' would erase the spelling distinction.
known_concerns: Dictation risk: very high because the intended spoken form does not determine whether the missing vowel is reflected in spelling.
The elision resembles dropped-vowel startup naming and may be perceived as malformed rather than deliberate.
notes: challenge_wave: form-saturation-a
challenge_cell: 1 derivation-clipping
form_mechanism: internal vowel elision from declare to dclare
stance: affirmative
scope: current
code_projection: hex=dclare; otp=:dclare; module=Dclare; mix=dclare; config=:dclare; telemetry=[:dclare].
current_embodiment: Dclare names the translation from a textual signature into a runtime-callable Elixir program.
horizon_embodiment: Dclare can cover explicit artifact declarations and optimizer lineage, though its spelling cost compounds across a larger portfolio.
candidate.rationale: Dclare exposes the tradeoff of preserving the audible declaration stem while removing an internal letter for compactness. It remains recognizable on the page and projects cleanly into an Elixir namespace.

candidate.etymology: Existing English prefix 'pre-' attached productively to 'declare'; used here as a software identity rather than claimed as a new word.
candidate.grammar: Prefixed ordinary verb and direct command: 'predeclare the task boundary'. As a title-case identity it is a converted noun, but the command reading is intended in prose and the namespace reading only in code.
known_concerns: Dictation risk: low in isolation, but speakers may collapse the middle syllables or write 'pre-declare'.
The name can imply declarations happen only before execution, while runtime context and iterative optimization also alter program behavior.

code_projection: hex=predeclare; otp=:predeclare; module=Predeclare; mix=predeclare; config=:predeclare; telemetry=[:predeclare].
current_embodiment: Predeclare describes signature-first construction before DSEx.call/2.
horizon_embodiment: Predeclare can require stable identities and types before instructions, demonstrations, tools, policies, schemas, code, or configuration enter an optimization campaign.
candidate.rationale: Predeclare makes sequence explicit: establish the typed task contract before runtime model behavior. It usefully challenges whether an identity can teach the workflow instead of merely naming a category.

candidate.etymology: Coined compound of English 'declare' and 'work'; no external source.
candidate.grammar: Suffixed compound category noun: 'declarework' is the work and artifact set produced by declaration. It is intentionally not a verb; prose needs 'write declarework' rather than the tempting but awkward 'declarework it'.
known_concerns: Dictation risk: medium because listeners may insert a space or hear 'declarer work'.
The compound is semantically broad but aesthetically heavy, and 'work' may imply a service or labor platform.

code_projection: hex=declarework; otp=:declarework; module=Declarework; mix=declarework; config=:declarework; telemetry=[:declarework].
current_embodiment: Declarework can denote the collection of signatures, examples, metrics, and persisted optimizer reports.
horizon_embodiment: Declarework naturally includes typed textual and code-bearing artifacts with provenance, feedback, and promotion history.

run.brief: Create a schema_version 1 identity portfolio for a pre-release Elixir/OTP library for declared, callable, measurable, optimizable LM programs, with a credible artifact horizon spanning instructions, demonstrations, tool descriptions, retrieval policies, playbooks, schemas, code fragments, and configuration. Treat it as neither an official DSPy port, static proof system, universal agent OS, provider SDK, guaranteed autonomous self-improvement system, safety product, standards body, institute, nor universal platform. Generate exactly 30 preserved candidates in three ten-item cells: ordinals 1-10 derivation-clipping across declaration-contract and boundary-translation using coined-category-noun and ordinary-verb forms for Elixir newcomers, international users, and future maintainers; ordinals 11-20 conversion-grammar across action-agency and care-stewardship-repair using ordinary-verb, ordinary-object, and phrase-imperative forms for affected publics and backend product engineers; ordinals 21-30 identity-grammar across plurality-ecosystem and infrastructure-logistics using namespace-led, institutional-community, and descriptive-category forms for future maintainers, buyers-founders, and OSS contributors. Use speech-first minimal pairs across full stem, front and back clipping, elision, prefix, suffix, and conversion, distinguishing recoverability from mere brevity. Test noun, verb, adjective, command, participle, and unavailable readings in support calls and code. Give identity candidates complete truthful role systems for master, descriptor, library, research, community, company, protocol, and product family, marking unsupported roles unavailable. Every candidate must have non-null pronunciation and grammar, honest etymology or explicit coined/no-source text, nonempty valid audience and architecture lenses, rationale, concerns, and separate challenge_wave, challenge_cell, form_mechanism, stance, scope, code_projection, current_embodiment, and horizon_embodiment notes. Use exactly six wildcard candidates, two per cell; exactly five affirmative candidates per cell; cells 1 and 7 have three ambivalent and two adverse candidates, cell 4 has two ambivalent and three adverse candidates; and every cell has four current, four horizon, and two both scopes.
